abstract: Understanding of episodic experience is not achieved at a single moment: it is a constructive process in which each new event is interpreted in light of relevant past events and prior knowledge. Yet this process is rarely measured as it unfolds, leaving unclear how the brain integrates past events to construct an evolving understanding of the present. We hypothesized that neural reactivation of past events at narrative event boundaries reflects not merely what people experience, but how they interpret their experience. We developed a behavioural paradigm that tracks, as a narrative unfolds, which past events people consider relevant for understanding each new event. By manipulating prior knowledge of the narrative's final plot twist, we examined the process by which the same experience yields different understanding. Across independent behavioural and fMRI cohorts, we found that prior knowledge similarly altered the variability and intersubject similarity of inferred relations between events and their neural reactivation at narrative event boundaries in the Default Mode Network. Moreover, stronger neural reactivation was associated with greater inferred relevance between events, and event pairs showing different behavioural relations across groups also showed corresponding differences in reactivation. These findings suggest that neural reactivation of past events at event boundaries reflects an unfolding inferential process that transforms shared experience into subjective understanding.
